summary: Defines terminology and lists requirements for resolving the context of emergency calls placed over VoIP and Internet multimedia systems. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: An Internet emergency call needs to reach the public safety answering point responsible for the caller's location. This RFC lists requirements for finding that destination and marking the call as an emergency.

questions: how are voip emergency calls routed
what is an emergency service urn
subtitle: Requirements for using location and service information to route Internet emergency calls

tldr.problem: Emergency-call arrangements built for the telephone network do not directly fit end-to-end Internet voice, text and multimedia calls, where access, application and location information may come from different parties.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines terminology and requirements for location, emergency service identifiers, and a mapping protocol that returns a suitable PSAP URI.
tldr.outcome: It is a requirements document, not a protocol specification. It notes LoST as a proposed mapping protocol and refers security analysis to a separate document.

today: RFC 5012 is Informational, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It sets requirements and does not define a mapping protocol.

sections.title: Purpose and Scope
sections.content:
The RFC covers emergency voice and non-voice calls, including text and multimedia, placed from an IP end system and delivered to an IP-capable public safety answering point (PSAP) over an IP network. It aims for at least the functionality of existing public switched telephone network emergency service while supporting Internet-based communication.

The mapping function uses a caller's location and an emergency service identifier to return one or more PSAP URIs. Identifying the caller and displaying the caller's location to the call taker are outside this document's scope. Its normative words describe mapping-protocol design requirements, not implementation or use requirements.
sections.plainLanguage: This document is about Internet calls that reach an IP-capable emergency answering point. It focuses on finding the right destination from location and service information, not on identifying the caller.

sections.title: People, Providers and Location
sections.content:
The RFC distinguishes the Internet Access Provider, which supplies physical and data-link connectivity; the Internet Service Provider, which supplies IP service; and the Application Service Provider or Voice Service Provider, which supplies applications or voice service. These roles may belong to different organizations. The emergency caller uses user equipment, and a call taker at a PSAP receives the request and may dispatch help.

Location may be civic, such as a street address, or geographic, such as coordinates in the WGS-84 datum. The document distinguishes a service number that a person dials from a service identifier used by protocols. A mapping client asks a mapping server to resolve a location to a PSAP URI or an intermediary responsible for that location.
sections.plainLanguage: Several organizations may provide Internet access, carry an application and supply voice service. The system also needs to distinguish the number a person dials from the protocol label that identifies an emergency service.

sections.title: How Location Reaches the Mapping Service
sections.content:
Location information may be available at the caller's device or obtained from the Internet Access Provider. The caller's user agent may ask a mapping service directly, or an emergency service routing proxy may ask on the caller's behalf and forward the call to a PSAP.

The RFC allows several roles to be combined in one organization or device. It notes that an application or voice provider may not know the caller's physical location when that provider is separate from the access provider. The mapping result is a URI usable by the signaling protocol, such as a SIP or SIPS URI.
sections.plainLanguage: The caller's device or a routing proxy can request a destination from the mapping service. The access provider may know the caller's location even when the application provider does not.

sections.title: High-Level and Location Requirements
sections.content:
The system should not assume that a voice provider exists, must account for international use, must not depend on one central administrative authority, and must support multiple media. The mapping protocol must return URIs usable with standard signaling, work without requiring enrollment in a mapping service, support common location formats, and not require the caller's true identity.

Location can be inserted by the user agent, referenced through a location pointer, or inserted by a proxy. The mapping protocol must support WGS-84 and by-value location delivery, report civic-location validation results, and handle two- and three-dimensional location. Successful civic-address validation must not be a condition for placing the emergency call.
sections.plainLanguage: The mapping system must work across regions and providers, support several kinds of calls and avoid requiring the caller's identity. An address that cannot be validated must not stop the emergency call.

sections.title: Service Identifiers and Mapping Requirements
sections.content:
An emergency service identifier lets signaling entities distinguish an emergency call and identify the requested service. The protocol must allow different services and an extensible identifier list, return a location-dependent emergency number, and allow user equipment to translate a home emergency number into a service identifier. If the requested service is unknown or unavailable, the call must still be routable to a generic emergency service, with the substitute identified.

Mapping can be caller-based or mediated by a proxy. The RFC requires a baseline protocol, incremental deployment, referrals to more qualified mapping servers, replicas for failover, and support for multiple PSAP URIs where needed. It also calls for minimizing call-setup delay and indicating data freshness. Security requirements are discussed in a separate document.
sections.plainLanguage: A device can look up a destination itself, or a proxy can do the lookup. If the exact emergency service is unavailable, the call must still reach a general emergency service.
